title: Optimal size of weak \(\varepsilon\)-nets for convex ranges
formal: For every fixed integer \(d\geq2\), determine the asymptotic order of \(f_d(\varepsilon)\) as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), up to multiplicative constants depending only on \(d\). Here \(f_d(\varepsilon)\) is the smallest worst-case number of auxiliary points required to hit every convex set containing at least an \(\varepsilon\) fraction of a finite point set in \(\mathbb R^d\).
why: Weak nets quantify how many representatives can preserve every large convex part of an arbitrary finite configuration. Sharp bounds would settle a basic gap in discrete geometry and clarify the geometric cost underlying transversal, selection and approximation results.
status_note: The extremal asymptotic question is open in the checked sources, including the higher-dimensional revision of December 2023. The bounded later-work review on 13 September 2026 did not find matching bounds for the stated family. Publication and revision dates are distinguished from the date of this status check.

sentences: A weak \(\varepsilon\)-net places auxiliary points so that every convex set containing at least an \(\varepsilon\) fraction of a given point set contains an auxiliary point.
The auxiliary points may lie anywhere in the ambient Euclidean space.
For each fixed dimension, the task is to determine the smallest worst-case net size as \(\varepsilon\) decreases.
The challenge comes from hitting all sufficiently populated convex regions simultaneously, regardless of the original configuration.
Sharp bounds would quantify how economically a finite set can represent its large convex subsets.

definitions: Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^d\) be any nonempty finite set of distinct points, and let \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\) be real. A weak \(\varepsilon\)-net is a finite set \(N\subset\mathbb R^d\) such that \(N\cap C\ne\varnothing\) for every convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) satisfying \(|P\cap C|\geq\varepsilon|P|\). A set is convex if it contains the segment joining any two of its points. All convex ranges, including unbounded and lower-dimensional ones, are allowed; no restriction to halfspaces, simplices or a given finite family is made. Equivalently it is enough to hit \(\operatorname{conv}(Q)\) for every \(Q\subseteq P\) with \(|Q|\geq\lceil\varepsilon|P|\rceil\), so using only closed convex ranges gives the same condition. Net points can lie anywhere in \(\mathbb R^d\) and need not belong to \(P\). Put \(w(P,\varepsilon)=\min\{|N|:N\text{ is a weak }\varepsilon\text{-net for }P\}\) and \(f_d(\varepsilon)=\sup_{P\subset\mathbb R^d,\,0<|P|<\infty}w(P,\varepsilon)\). The minimum exists since \(N=P\) is feasible. The supremum ranges over every size and configuration with the same fixed dimension and accuracy; a bound depending on \(|P|\) is not a bound on \(f_d\). The weak-net theorem ensures \(f_d(\varepsilon)<\infty\). There is no general-position, rational-coordinate, uniform-measure-on-space, algorithmic or randomized guarantee in the target: the only measure is the uniform counting measure on the given finite set. The problem measures extremal cardinality, not construction time.
answer_criterion: Supply a noncircular rate \(G_d(\varepsilon)\) and a complete Lean-checked proof that for each fixed \(d\geq2\) there are \(c_d,C_d,\varepsilon_d>0\) with \(c_dG_d(\varepsilon)\leq f_d(\varepsilon)\leq C_dG_d(\varepsilon)\) whenever \(0<\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_d\). Upper bounds must cover all finite configurations; lower bounds must establish configurations requiring the matching order. Constants may depend on dimension but not on accuracy or input size. The exponent alone, bounds missing logarithmic factors, or a solution only for the plane do not characterize the stated family.

context_blocks.text: Rubin’s paper explicitly identifies the true asymptotic behavior of weak-net size in every fixed dimension at least two as an outstanding problem. The cardinality function above is the source’s extremal target, with its counting, rounding and range conventions made explicit.

A strong net is required to choose its points from the input. Allowing auxiliary points is essential for arbitrary convex ranges: arguments for bounded-complexity range families do not automatically supply weak nets for all convex sets.

Bukh, Matoušek and Nivasch prove the general lower bound \(f_d(\varepsilon)=\Omega_d(\varepsilon^{-1}\log^{d-1}(1/\varepsilon))\). In particular, already in the plane a universal bound proportional to \(1/\varepsilon\) is impossible.

Rubin improves the planar upper bound to \(O_\gamma(\varepsilon^{-3/2-\gamma})\) for every fixed \(\gamma>0\). The constant can depend on \(\gamma\); this theorem is not the assertion of an \(O(\varepsilon^{-3/2})\) bound with a uniform constant.

Rubin’s higher-dimensional work, including its December 2023 revision, improves the previously known upper bounds in all fixed dimensions at least three. Those bounds still do not match the lower bound above. Their dependence on dimension does not turn the problem into a joint large-dimension asymptotic question.

The same net must hit all heavy convex ranges simultaneously. Choosing a different auxiliary point after seeing each range would be a different and trivial requirement. This simultaneous coverage is what makes the extremal bound relevant to geometric transversals and sampling.
